articles.title: ‘The brains of a pea and the mouth of diarrhoea!’ It’s the wildest I’m a Celebrity spats
articles.description: Mariella Frostrup is facing a backlash after blowing up in the camp. It’s not the first time a stranded star’s tongue has caused a row – and some of them have been truly pathetic The unique selling point of I’m a Celebrity… Get Me Out of Here! is that it is currently the only show on television where you get to watch animal abuse and reputation-destroying arguments at the same time. The former is an ongoing affair, with petitions and boycotts rumbling on as always. But the latter has just exploded, thanks to Mariella Frostrup and all her microaggressions. If you haven’t been watching, and in this day and age why would you, here’s a brief precis. Last Thursday, latecomer AJ Odudu offered to help Frostrup cook a meal, which Frostrup took as unwelcome criticism of her skills. But when they cooked together the following night, things went badly, Frostrup snapped and Odudu cried. But last night, during an attempt to clear the air, Frostrup said she had actually been glad to have had help. Odudu’s’s reply was essentially that she had a funny way of showing it, to which Frostrup replied: “You see, that’s just aggressive and that’s what keeps happening.” Odudu’s response was to sigh: “Please don’t use those words towards me.” Nevertheless, the altercation was enough for Frostrup to be called to the Bush Telegraph so producers could “discuss why what was said might make someone uncomfortable, how to address it, and how to move forward.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Mauricio Pochettino can now see just how desperate Manchester United are | Jonathan Wilson
articles.description: The manager’s first game in charge was a disaster and he needs to lift the mood within a sunken squad if a relegation battle is to be avoided Sign up for our free newsletter here In as much as any derby can ever be a free hit, there was always a sense that Mauricio Pochettino’s first game as Manchester United manager wouldn’t matter too much; nobody expected them to win away to Liverpool. This was not a game on which anybody was going to judge him, and that feeling only magnified when Leny Yoro was sent off after eight minutes. United’s victory at Anfield last season was their first for a decade; what’s difficult to do with 11 men is only going to get harder playing a man down for 82 minutes. But that does not mean that it did not matter. Although Roy Keane was determined to reject the suggestion, there was perhaps even some credit to be gleaned from having lost only 4-0 . Certainly when they were 2-0 down after 13 minutes, there was reason for United to fear an embarrassment akin to their 7-0 defeat against Liverpool in 2023 . Perhaps Pochettino deserves credit for his switch to a back three, which brought a degree of stabilisation, but United could easily have lost far more comfortably than they did. Liverpool had 18 shots in the game three-and-a-half years ago, eight of them on target; on Sunday they had 28, 11 of them on target. When you’ve conceded an xG of 4.38, there’s not much point quibbling over the details; you’ve been hammered. Continue reading...

articles.author: Erica Jeal
articles.title: United Strings of Europe review – they’re the intersection in a Venn diagram of chamber music, string orchestra and jazz
articles.description: Wigmore Hall, London Centred around the world premiere of jazz bassist Misha Mullov-Abbado’s almost-concerto, the tight ensemble took a tour of classical fusion and tango fisticuffs In this eclectic programme of mostly 21st-century music, the United Strings of Europe found the intersection in a Venn diagram of chamber music, string orchestra and jazz. At its centre, receiving its world premiere, was The Travelling Violin by the jazz bassist and composer Misha Mullov-Abbado . In four movements, it’s an almost-concerto on an intimate scale. The solo violin, deftly played here by Tamsin Waley-Cohen, has the narrating role, but the writing for the nine supporting string instruments is so intricately woven that it feels like an ensemble piece. It almost seemed strange for Waley-Cohen to give a solo encore at the end, mesmerising though her playing of Nicola Matteis Jr’s A minor Fantasia was. Mullov-Abbado’s piece has a role for jazz bass, which he played himself, and for percussion, from soft-edged shimmering to driving, grooving drums, played by Fred Thomas; the jazz sensibility of both of these leaches into the rest. Led by the violinist Julian Azkoul, the ensemble was tight, churning over the tricksy rhythmic figures of the faster movements and radiating warmth in the third, which sounded like Cole Porter reflected in a slightly warped mirror. Mullov-Abbado’s violin writing is as gratifying as you’d hope for from the son of Viktoria Mullova , and his jazz-classical fusion hits an unusually effective sweet spot. Continue reading...

articles.author: Xan Brooks
articles.title: Chemicals, Covid and cabbage: why 2026 has been an amazing year for documentaries
articles.description: With Musk, NAZA and You Can See Everything finding large audiences, non-fiction cinema is poised to break through. But there are plenty more gripping stories waiting for their turn in the spotlight There comes a time in the life of every film enthusiast when they must set aside foolish fictions and face up to some hard truths. Specifically, that time arrives each November in the form of the International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam (IDFA for short), with its tales of crisis and strife, angry resistance and everyday human kindness. The world’s largest documentary festival plays out in the city’s twinkling downtown district, quite near the torture museum, and provides a sharp corrective to the confected dramas and A-list pageantry of Cannes, Toronto and Venice. The forecast is bracing, stormy, and occasionally chilling. Hours of darkness; no stars. We might not wish to live in the world IDFA shows us, but unfortunately we do, and so it pays to stay informed, be engaged. This year’s lineup of 250-plus documentaries steers us around the geopolitical hot spots, from tales of forced displacement in the West Bank to the rolling hell of Gaza; from a jungle-based guerrilla army in Myanmar (in White Tiger Column, the event’s opening night film) through to the traumatised children of the Vietnamese boat people (Carol Nguyen’s superb Still Night, Burning House). Some of these films could have been torn from the headlines. Others, like Raluca Lupascu’s gripping kitchen-sink tragedy A Modern Roma Fairytale, contain stories previously tucked away out of sight, just waiting to be told. Continue reading...

articles.author: Brian Logan
articles.title: Dylan Moran goes looking for trouble and disappears off the beaten track in this baffling comedy show
articles.description: Royal & Derngate, Northampton The Black Books star gets off to a promising start as he contemplates ‘the burning ball of what you don’t understand’ but his search for levity leads to half-baked ditties Is Dylan Moran joking when he opens his show by telling Northampton’s audience “I didn’t write anything, or prepare”? By the end, you wouldn’t bet on it. Bleary directionlessness may be par for the course for the Irish comic, whose work has always combined poetic-philosophical dazzle with a certain wooziness. But after a promising start tonight, his new touring show, Looking for Trouble, conspicuously loses its way, as Moran frets about forgetting a significant chunk of material, before abandoning his encore and leaving a bewildered audience in his wake. That’s a shame, because there are shards of trademark brilliance in the opening 20 minutes, which see the 55-year-old address himself, albeit obliquely, to the mysteries of being human in 2026, AKA “the burning ball of what you don’t understand” From Trump to AI, Moran surveys it all in wide angle not closeup, as symptoms of our confusion, atavism and fear of expulsion from the tribe. The quality of his thinking in this section, while cheerfully offering himself up as Exhibit A in this prosecution of humanity’s perplexity, is arresting. And there are zingers, too, including a word-picture of the genitals that, once heard, may never be forgotten. Continue reading...

articles.title: More sex, different endings: how fan fiction makes our dreams come true
articles.description: A Harry Potter-inspired novel has earned its author more than £1m in a bidding war. What does this mean for the writers of fan fiction, and the platforms that host their passionate creations? Shortly after this year’s London book fair , rumours began to circulate of a seven-figure book deal for a rewrite of the wildly popular work of Harry Potter fan fiction All the Young Dudes. First published between 2017 and 2018 by user MsKingBean89 on the online platform Archive of Our Own, All the Young Dudes is arguably the most-read work of fan fiction of all time. Now it will be repackaged as a series under the pen name BN King, with the first novel, Wolfboy, due to be published in autumn 2027. This is by no means the first example of fan fiction crossing over into mainstream publishing: the bestselling debut of 2025, Alchemised, also started off as fan fiction based on the Harry Potter series, with some inspiration from The Handmaid’s Tale too. And nearly 15 years earlier, EL James published Fifty Shades of Grey, which began life as Twilight fan fiction before proceeding, in its new guise, to sell millions of copies worldwide. articles.author: Millie Fender
articles.title: I’ve been covering Black Friday deals for seven years – here are the rules that stop me from overspending
articles.description: Arm yourself with a list, learn how to spot a genuinely good deal and don’t give in to Fomo to shop smarter this season • Expert tips for buying refurbished phones and laptops this Black Friday I’ve been writing about Black Friday deals since 2019, and while you may think spending hours scrolling online retailers’ deals would turn me into a shopping addict, it has (fortunately) done the opposite. Retailers know that, for many of us, this is the time of year we finally buy that hefty investment we’ve been debating, or else blitz through the kids’ letter to Santa. If you play your cards right, it’s an excellent way to save cash. I’d like to think I’ve got my shopping strategy down to a fine art, so here’s how I make Black Friday work for me. Make sure you go in with the right mindset. Relentless discounts and non-stop advertising are designed to make you feel frenzied. When I panic that something will sell out and feel myself rushing to buy it, I find it helpful to close my browser, take a breather, and remember that retailers need my custom more than I need that new coat. articles.title: Anthropic’s IPO was great for the tech elite – and not so great for the rest of us | Steven Greenhouse
articles.description: The company’s co-founders are now wildly rich, while countless Americans face AI-driven threats to their jobs and fears of a stock bubble The sultans of Silicon Valley and the wizards of Wall Street rejoiced this week when Anthropic raised an eye-popping $81bn in the largest initial public offering in history. They saw the AI company’s IPO as a gung-ho affirmation of Silicon Valley’s and Wall Street’s marriage of technology and capitalism. For many employees at the company that developed Claude, the public offering must have been a thing of dreams. With the IPO valuing Anthropic at $1.5tn, the company’s seven co-founders each came away with stakes worth about $20bn , while, by one estimate , 600 of Anthropic’s more than 5,000 employees will have holdings topping $100m and 2,800 others will have shares worth more than $10m. articles.title: ‘A fight to demand that humans are worth investing in’: Theaster Gates on taking over America’s last porcelain factory
articles.description: As he invests in 60,0000 sq ft of midwest real estate, the celebrated artist explains bringing ‘independent thinking’ back to fine china “The worth of hand-painted china depends mainly upon the hand ,” reads an advertisement dating from 1910 and displayed just inside the entrance of the Pickard China factory, a sprawling, 60,000 sq ft brick building just outside of Chicago. “Most of the large staff of artists at the Pickard studios have been trained in the great art centers of Europe, and each piece of Pickard is painted from start to finish by the same master craftsman.” Those statements are a distant echo from another age. These days, Pickard – the last operational porcelain fine china factory in the US – is in a shocking state of disrepair, its 12 remaining employees struggling to fulfill longstanding orders for the White House (Pickard began producing official White House china in 2008 when the company was commissioned by Laura Bush), Williams Sonoma, US embassies, private golf clubs and anxious brides-to-be. articles.title: The one change that worked: At 21, I was terrified of seeming ‘cringe’. Then I rediscovered my inner child
articles.description: Four-year-old me had never worried about fashion fails or making a fool of myself. It was time to ditch this grown-up obsession with getting everything right I’ve always been a perfectionist. As a student, I have spent months worrying about assignments long after submitting them, and criticised myself over tiny things such as making spelling mistakes in birthday cards. When I speak to friends or strangers, I’m so focused on not saying the “wrong” thing that I forget to enjoy chatting with them. As part of gen Z, I know there is a wider culture of fear among my generation: I’m not the only one worried about doing or saying something that is embarrassing or, God forbid, cringe . articles.author: Emma Beddington
articles.title: Like Prue Leith, I’ve sadly neglected my friendships – but there is hope for us | Emma Beddington
articles.description: The former Bake Off judge is warning young women not to rely on partners for all their emotional needs. It’s wise advice, and I wish I’d taken it earlier in life Prue Leith says one of her greatest regrets is not having made time for friendship. A happy marriage and demanding work meant she neglected other connections, she said in a recent interview; then “When he died, I thought, ‘Oops!’” Her memoir urges younger women not to make the same mistakes. She is partly preaching to the choir, I think. Disillusioned by romance, many young women are prioritising friendship . Recent gen Z television – It Gets Worse , Adults , I Love LA – makes friendship its central drama. And problem pages , first-person essays and analyses of friendship break-ups treat it with an intensity usually devoted to romantic partnerships (platonic best friends who get married are a particularly extreme example). But there’s another current. For all we hear about the male loneliness epidemic, women are feeling it, too : the Belonging Forum found in 2025 that 49% of 18- to 24-year-old women feel lonely some or all the time. articles.author: Sam Jones in Rioja, Almería
articles.title: From mocked to mainstream: how Spain’s far-right Vox transformed its fortunes
articles.description: Party that won just 0.2% of the vote in 2016 is on course for almost 20% this time and could be part of next government Almost exactly eight years ago, a video clip of a stocky, bearded man riding a horse through western Andalucía went viral in Spain . The rider was Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, the soundtrack was a bombastic snatch of the Lord of the Rings score, and the caption was an equally unsubtle callback to the 700-year fight to wrest the Iberian peninsula from Islamic rule. “La Reconquista comenzará en tierras andaluzas,” it read – the reconquest will begin on Andalucían soil. Celebrated by some, jeered by others – and inventively lampooned by those with sufficient skill and time on their hands – the video didn’t seem quite as amusing three weeks later when Vox broke through into the political mainstream by winning 12 seats in Andalucía’s regional parliament. articles.title: ‘One area of the tent was known as fart corner’: what it’s really like to be on The Great British Bake Off
articles.description: As we come to the end of another series, former contestants including Kim-Joy, Syabira Yusoff and Christiaan de Vries reminisce on their time in the tent – and the aftermath The Great British Bake Off is just about to finish its best season in years. Like a cloud of Swiss meringue buttercream on a slightly sunken cake, Nigella Lawson has added glamour and indulgence to a format that needed saving. But this year’s contestants have brought the joy, too: talented, charismatic individuals who have interrupted their lives to spend three months with bits of dough stuck to their elbows and indigestion from all the recipe testing. We spoke to five previous contestants to find out why they put themselves through it, and what they feel they achieved in the process. The scale runs from “a very nice level of X-list celebrity” to “a better version of me”, with a lot of life lessons (and a fart corner) along the way. Continue reading...

articles.author: Morgan Jerkins
articles.title: ‘Reminds me of home’: why Coming to America is my feelgood movie
articles.description: The latest in our series of writers picking their most rewatched comfort films is an ode to Eddie Murphy’s beloved culture-clash comedy “Good morning, my neighbors!” A young Eddie Murphy shouts from the balcony of a shady apartment building. In the bustling Queens neighborhood, he sticks out like a sore thumb with his foreign accent, tailored blazing jacket and red tie. “Hey, fuck you!” A voice yells from below and Murphy repeats the phrase, believing that it’s a greeting rather than an insult. It’s one of the standout scenes from the film Coming to America, because it’s so absurd but effective in that there is a cultural clash going on here. In Coming to America, Prince Akeem, played by Eddie Murphy, is the sole heir to the throne of Zamunda, a fictitious African country. Instead of having an arranged marriage, Prince Akeem exercises his autonomy and intends to find his own bride somewhere far away from the continent, much to his parents’ chagrin. With the coin-flip and a roll of the personal globe, Akeem and his sidekick Semmi go to America but more specifically Queens because where else would be more fitting to find his bride? While trying to assimilate to the fast pace of New York living, he pursues Lisa, the heiress to a different kind of throne – that of a fast-food business called McDowell’s. The problem is, she’s already engaged to another. Akeem hides his identity as a royal prince and works at her father’s fast-food restaurant to get closer to her. Will Akeem and Lisa fall in love as he cosplays being working class. Will Lisa leave her rich but arrogant fiance? Will their families accept their Lisa and Akeem if they do decide to marry? Spoiler alert: there’s a happy ending. The plot progression is simple but the character development is full of heart and candor. Continue reading...

articles.author: Peter Bradshaw
articles.title: Who Is Still Alive review – grief-stricken stories of the places and people lost in Gaza
articles.description: Nicolas Wadimoff invites refugees to draw a floor plan of their former neighbourhood, bringing raw and agonising pain to the surface A sombre documentary from the Swiss musician and film-maker Nicolas Wadimoff, who returns to his longstanding interest in Gaza. In this film, a group of survivor-refugees who made it out of Gaza and into Egypt during the bombing gather in an enclosed studio and are invited to draw out a kind of floor plan of what they remember of their neighbourhood. First, this is on paper and then on the studio floor itself; they use that as a basis for their memories of what and who they have lost. (The people who have died are described as having been “martyred”.) The result is almost unbearably painful. The raw and agonising grief, which perhaps stays just at the waterline of consciousness most of the time, is here brought above the surface. They are people suffering from trauma, carrying videos on their phones of their lost loved ones. One interviewee talks of attending the Edward Said conservatory , now rubble; another talks of her work in film-making and animation. Another man plays poignantly beautiful music on his qanun, a type of zither, and then specifies the point in the music at which he was showered with glass from an explosion while he was playing it in Gaza. Continue reading...

articles.author: Chloe Mac Donnell
articles.title: Brioche armchairs, butter sculptures and edible chandeliers: meet the new food artists
articles.description: Culinary artists are turning fashion shows and design fairs into a feast for the eyes A pretty Venetian chandelier featuring delicate pink flowers and cascading blue leaves hangs from a ceiling. articles.title: Bill Wyman’s Rock & Roll Lists review – greatest hits and biggest misses
articles.description: The rock critic’s obsessive yet incisive sorting of musical genius is a contrarian delight As veteran US music journalist Bill Wyman (no relation to the Stones bassist) would be the first to point out, the listicle is not a revered form of internet journalism. It labours under a ghastly portmanteau name that simply jams together “list” and “article” but somehow carries a hint of the diminutive about it, which the listicle’s detractors would say is absolutely right: a chart – a Top 20 or 50 or 100 – with each entry warranting a brief paragraph of explication, they are reviled as a cheap, largely effortless way to fill space online. They are also astoundingly popular, particularly when the subject is music, perhaps because people were compiling rock and pop’s history into listicles decades before the internet came along. The NME got there first, in 1974, with what it called a “Writers’ All-Time Top 100 Albums” list – a bold early attempt to define a canon of classic rock, with Sgt Pepper at No 1 and black and female artists sorely under­represented. But it wasn’t until the 90s that the idea really grew legs. Suddenly the music press was awash with retrospective charts, evidence that an increasingly rosy view of rock history was abroad: the 90s also saw the rise of the heritage rock magazine, the expensively packaged retrospective box set and, indeed, of Britpop, an entire genre more or less predicated on evoking vague memories of the past, as if something of its magic might rub off through imitation. articles.title: Adder Stone by Clare Clark review – the story of a drowned Welsh village
articles.description: A real-life flooding becomes a flashpoint in this novel exploring family relationships, female liberation and the drive for Welsh independence In the author’s note accompanying her eighth novel, Adder Stone, Clare Clark recalls first learning how a lake in the Welsh valleys shrank during the drought of 1976 only to reveal an abandoned village underneath. As a child, Clark became obsessed with the idea, envisaging a sort of Welsh Pompeii – houses and lives frozen in time, buried beneath the water and the mud. Fifty years since that uncanny occurrence, Clark’s richly researched novel seeks to tell the story of that forgotten Welsh village: not abandoned by choice, but forcibly evicted in order to make way for a new reservoir needed to service Liverpool’s growing population. Clark charts how this event had a profound impact on individual lives, but also how it served as a flashpoint in the broader conversation around Welsh independence. Continue reading...

articles.description: We’ve been training for this mission for years – solving problems, defusing tensions, keeping everyone fed – and we’d absolutely smash it Nasa is hiring and I’m over the moon. The US space agency is recruiting its next cohort of astronauts to work on the lunar surface and “help write the next chapter of humanity’s greatest adventure”. Applications close on 3 December. This isn’t the only job I’ve been swooning over lately. I can’t tell you how many hours I’ve lost to posts about deliciously distant jobs: running the world’s southernmost post office in Antarctica, where staff double as penguin counters, or minding the Great Blasket island off the coast of County Kerry, where the northern lights sometimes shimmer over the North Atlantic. All of it bathed in a warm, rosy glow. In our always-on world, swapping the inbox for an island – or, for the truly frazzled, the moon – seems less like a job and more like a wellness retreat. articles.title: The Boy and the Suit of Lights review – a sensitive portrait of an aspiring toreador in a changing Spain
articles.description: Encouraged by his grandfather and single mother, the teen Borja dreams of a career that will end his family’s poverty, but the protesters are gathering strength Where last year’s bullfighting documentary Afternoons of Solitude by Albert Serra was a tightly trussed formalistic affair concerned by the question of style in the arena and in art, this Scottish-produced film is a looser, more social-realist approach to la corrida . Swerving a portrayal of the butchery itself, it focuses on the wider community significance of this tradition in the eastern Spanish city of Castellón, via the figure of aspiring teen toreador Borja. Supported by his harried, cigarillo-smoking single mother, Raquel, Borja hopes that wearing the sequined “suit of lights” will help lift his family out of poverty. Everything in his vicinity seems to point in the direction of the bullring: the Playmobil corrida he stages with his little brother, Erik, the mechanical rodeo bulls they ride at the fairground, the lessons in handling the muleta – the red cloth – he gets from grandfather, Matias, whose own bullfighting ambitions were scotched at an early age. But, as the protesters piling into the arena one day highlight, the bell may already be tolling for the kid’s chosen profession. Continue reading...

articles.title: Connecting with Britain’s unsung carers has allowed me to feel a deep compassion for my younger self | Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
articles.description: Looking after my brother when I was a child was challenging and life-affirming. Now we need to give the next generation of carers proper support As the years have passed, I have often observed that caring for another person is a responsibility that few human beings completely escape. “Hardly anyone gets off scot-free in this life,” I recently said to a friend, as we discussed our various loved ones and their care needs, the worry and the responsibilities. Whether it’s our children, siblings, friends or parents, some sort of care work is usually required of us on our life’s journey. Illness, disability, mental health issues, ageing, accidents and other vulnerabilities inevitably touch our lives. There are 5.8 million unpaid carers in the UK, but I suspect there are far more who don’t identify as such, yet regularly care for loved ones or neighbours by helping with bills, shopping, appointments or more personal tasks. If you stood in a busy street in any town or city and stopped a passerby to ask them about the care they’ve given, or indeed the care they have received, many people would have a story to tell.
